newsitem.title: UK: Distant galaxies older than we thought - astronomers.
newsitem.headline: Distant galaxies older than we thought - astronomers.

text.p: Images of the faintest galaxies ever seen show they are much older than astronomers thought and date back 10 billion years, British scientists said on Wednesday.
The blue-tinted galaxies were seen during an unusually long look at an apparently blank area of sky by the orbiting Hubble Space Telescope.
Astronomers at the University of Durham analysed exposures taken by the camera and compared them with ground-based observations.
In a report in the science journal Nature they said the changes in the light made over its journey in time and space showed the galaxies were much older than previously believed.
"What you are doing is using the Hubble Deep Field picture as a sort of a time machine," said Tom Shanks, who led the study.
"These very faint galaxies are very blue," he said in a telephone interview. Blue-tinged light means the galaxies are young and still forming.

Another change in light, known as red shift, told the astronomers that the galaxies were very, very far away. Red shift in light works like the Doppler effect on sound, as when the sound of a train passing rises, peaks and falls.

"The light has taken 10 billion years to get to us, so you are looking at the history of when these galaxies were born," Shanks said. "You can essentially put a date on the epoch of galaxy formation."
The Hubble team agreed last December to take a long look at a dark part of the sky near the constellation Ursa Major, also known as the Big Dipper or the Plough.
They found a region packed full of ancient galaxies, dim because they are so far away.
The Royal Astronomical Society said the Durham group's observations would help astronomers settle the question of how old the universe was.
Estimates range from about nine billion to 15 billion years old but some stars have been found that seem to be even older than this.
Shanks said the pictures also will help astronomers figure out how galaxies evolved to the form they are in now, like the spiralling Milky Way, which includes our own solar system.

"In these pictures you also see brighter, more nearby galaxies. As you come forward you see the galaxies in the adolescent stage," Shanks said. "We are tracking the history of how a galaxy evolves, almost right the way back to the Big Bang."

Earlier this month U.S. astronomers using the Hubble telescope said they had identified "blobs" in the distant sky that they believed were the basic building blocks of galaxies. They dated back 11 billion years.
